extraction.name: MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
extraction.description: MMMU is a benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected in three stages. First, 30 subjects from six disciplines were selected based on the principle that visual inputs are commonly adopted. Second, over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in these majors were recruited as annotators to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators adhered to copyright and license regulations and were advised to select questions without immediately available answers. This process resulted in a diverse collection of 13K questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Multimodal questions collected from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, free online resources, and lecture materials across six disciplines and 30 subjects.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with the design criteria due to their simplistic nature, were excluded from the benchmark. The dataset was divided into a few-shot development set (5 questions per subject), a validation set (~900 questions), and a test set (10.5K questions).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Two steps of data cleaning were performed. First, lexical overlap and source URL similarity were employed to identify potential duplicate problems, which were then reviewed by authors to eliminate duplications. Second, problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format. Third, authors categorized problems into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard), and approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students specializing in the relevant majors were recruited as annotators. They collected multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, and created new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoid data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution, and select questions without immediately available answers. Each question was annotated with fields including question type, question text, answer options (for multiple-choice), correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation (if available). A secondary review team vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence, and regular audits of random samples were conducted.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A user-friendly web interface for data annotation and verification was developed by Tianyu Zheng.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Error analysis was conducted on 150 randomly sampled error instances from GPT-4V's predictions, analyzed by expert annotators who identified root causes of mispredictions. Errors were categorized as: Perceptual Errors (35%), Lack of Knowledge (29%), Reasoning Errors (26%), Textual Understanding Error (4%), Rejection to Answer (3%), Annotation Error (2%), and Answer Extraction Error (1%).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students (including co-authors) from various disciplines and subjects, specializing in the relevant majors. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent a wide range of experts in the corresponding 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: MMOCR (for OCR), LLaVA-1.5 (for image captioning as baseline augmentation)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset has a live-updating leaderboard available at https://mmmu-benchmark.github.io/#leaderboard. Multiple versions have been released (V1: Nov. 27, V2: Dec. 18, V3: Dec. 21, V4: June 13). Version change logs document updates including addition of new model results, corrections of typos, and dataset refinements.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: MMMU is designed to monitor progress towards Expert AGI, defined as AI systems reaching at least the 90th percentile of skilled adults in a broad range of tasks. The benchmark addresses the societal importance of tracking AI progress, as Expert AGI could lead to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. The authors caution that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI but should be a necessary criterion for an Expert AGI system.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases. GPT-4V exhibits a bias towards text, prioritizing textual information over visual inputs. The benchmark's focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. Open-source models generalize poorly towards less common image types like geometric shapes, music sheets, and chemical structures.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI as there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and '90th percentile of skilled adults,' nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. The benchmark covers only subjects where visual inputs are commonly adopted, ruling out subjects like law and linguistics.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing and benchmarking of large multimodal models (LMMs) on expert-level multimodal understanding and reasoning tasks. The dataset is split into a few-shot development set (for in-context learning demonstrations), a validation set (for hyperparameter selection), and a test set (for evaluation). It is intended to stimulate the community to build next-generation multimodal foundation models towards expert artificial general intelligence.
